title: Introducing Arrays
objective: Create an array and read individual elements by index.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only; this book chapter covers both arrays and objects — Code Forge splits them into separate chapters. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: An array stores a sequence of values in a single variable. You build one with square brackets, separating items with commas, like const crew = ["Nyx", "Bram", "Fen"]. An array can hold any type of value, and the items keep the order you gave them.

Each item has an index — a numbered position JavaScript uses to find it. Indexing starts at 0, so crew[0] is the first item and crew[1] is the second. Asking for an index that doesn't exist returns undefined instead of raising an error, which is a common source of quiet bugs — always double check an index is really in range.

Unlike some languages, JavaScript arrays do not support negative indices. crew[-1] does not give you the last item — it looks for a property literally named "-1" and returns undefined. To reach the last item, use crew[crew.length - 1], since .length always holds the current number of items.
explanation.rule: Array indices start at 0. There is no negative indexing in JavaScript — use arr[arr.length - 1] to reach the last item.

examples.title: Building a Roster
examples.note: crew[0] reads the first item. crew[crew.length - 1] reads the last item without needing to know the array's exact length in advance.

examples.title: An Out-of-Range Index
examples.note: There is no item at index 5, so JavaScript returns undefined rather than throwing an error.

checks.question: const arr = [10, 20, 30]; what does arr[-1] give you?

feedback.correct: Correct — JavaScript has no negative indexing, so arr[-1] just looks for a property named "-1" and finds nothing.
feedback.incorrect: JavaScript arrays don't support negative indices the way some other languages do. arr[-1] returns undefined.

assignment.title: Squad Report
assignment.brief: Write squadReport(members) that logs the squad leader (the first member) and the rear guard (the last member).
requirements: Log the last member, found using members.length (not a hardcoded index).

requirementChecks.label: Uses .length to find the last member

assignment.outputCheckLabel: squadReport([...]) logs the first member then the last member

hints: members[0] reads the first item in the array.
The last item's index is one less than the array's length.
members[members.length - 1] works no matter how many members are passed in.
Log the first member on one line, then the last member on the next.
